beats.prose:
The salvage scanner hummed its familiar pattern across the spectral display, each pulse a small affirmation that the Iron Ghost was still moving, still hunting, still alive in the way that mattered. Kael watched the data scroll across the holographic feed, his neural implant translating the raw sensor input into something his eyes could parse: rock compositions, thermal signatures, the occasional glint of metal half-buried in ice. It was work. It was rhythm. It was the thing that came after thinking had stopped being useful.

Seven years of this. Seven years of running the same route through the Kuiper Belt's outer edges, where the Corporate Defense Alliance's patrols grew thin and the salvage was sparse enough to keep him moving but not so scarce that he had to venture closer to the inner system. Seven years of solitude that he had convinced himself was mastery—the perfect distillation of a life stripped down to its functional minimum.

The implant stuttered.

For a fraction of a second, the scanner feed fractured. Instead of rock composition, he saw static. Instead of thermal data, he heard something beneath the static—a sound like screaming compressed through a faulty filter, then gone. Kael's hand tightened on the armrest. He ran a diagnostic check on the neural interface, watching the cascade of green confirmations scroll past. System nominal. All functions optimal. The stutter had lasted maybe half a second. Nothing.

He turned back to the scanner.

The salvage operator's seat was worn thin in the center from seven years of his weight. The Iron Ghost's bridge was a scatter of jury-rigged components and faded mission patches from a life that no longer existed. The coffee in his cup—he couldn't remember when he'd poured it—had gone cold enough to form a skin on the surface. He drank it anyway. The taste was bitter and metallic, which meant the water recycler was starting to fray again. He made a mental note to replace the cartridge when he next made port, knowing he wouldn't.

The salvage scanner returned to its steady pulse. Rock. Ice. More rock. The void was patient, and the void asked nothing.

But the stuttering came again. A longer fracture this time, the neural implant catching on something in the background radiation—or so his rational mind insisted, the part of him that had learned to translate anomaly into meaninglessness. The screaming came through clearer. Multiple voices. Overlapping. Male voices, most of them. Voices he had trained beside. Voices he had given orders to. Voices he had not heard in seven years except in the hour before sleep, when the numbness wore thin enough to let them through.

Kael killed the diagnostic loop and forced his attention back to the scanner. The next salvage site was three hours of drift away. A metallic signature that might be copper, might be worthless. The work was always worthless. That was the point. Nothing that mattered could hurt you if you only pursued things that didn't matter.

The implant went quiet.

The silence was worse. The silence meant he was thinking again, and thinking meant the routine was broken. Kael reached for the navigation console and adjusted their heading, pushing the Iron Ghost a fraction of a degree starboard toward the thermal anomaly. The engines' hum shifted pitch, a small song of acceleration. The ship was responding. The ship was always responsive. It asked nothing and demanded nothing and would follow him to the edge of the system or into the sun with equal indifference.

He was alone. He had arranged it carefully, methodically, over seven years of deliberate choices. This was the architecture of survival. This was the only shape that had kept him breathing.

The scanner hummed. The void waited. And beneath both, so faint that denial remained possible, something was beginning to wake.

The scanner's pulse shifted.

Not the steady cadence Kael had tuned out over seven years—this was different. A rhythm buried beneath the normal frequency sweep, so faint it might have been a glitch in the sensor array, except the pattern repeated. Three pulses. Pause. Three pulses again. The kind of rhythm that didn't occur in nature. The kind that meant something.

Kael's hand moved to the scanner controls before his mind had finished processing why. The display adjusted, filtering out background radiation, and the signal resolved into something cleaner. A source point thirty-two degrees off the current heading, distance approximately four light-seconds. The coordinates registered as empty space on every corporate database he could access through the Iron Ghost's systems. No mining claims. No research stations. No reason for anything to be transmitting from that position.

Three pulses. Pause. Three pulses.

He should ignore it. The rational calculus was simple: unknown signals meant corporate traps, pirate beacons, or the detritus of dead ships broadcasting their final moments on automated loops. Salvage operators who chased ghosts in empty space didn't come back. That rule had kept him alive through seven years when staying alive was the only goal that mattered.

Kael pulled up the signal analysis. The encryption was unlike anything in his neural implant's reference database—not corporate military grade, not pirate-simple, not even the old Earth-standard protocols that still haunted some of the derelict stations in the belt. The signal itself was ancient. He could feel that somehow, reading it off the screen the way a musician reads the age of an instrument from the depth of its wood. This thing had been transmitting for longer than human civilization had been in space.

Three pulses. Pause.

His jaw tightened. He ran a second diagnostic on the neural implant's translation matrix, watching the cascade of confirmations again. Everything nominal. The signal was real. The encryption was real. And something in the rhythm of it felt like it was reaching toward him specifically, the way a hand in darkness reaches toward a voice.

He told himself it was curiosity. Just curiosity—the reflex of a salvage operator spotting something that didn't fit. He told himself he was running the numbers: distance, fuel consumption, probability of recovery value. He told himself a hundred rational things while his hands were already moving across the navigation console, already plotting a course toward those coordinates, already calculating the intercept vector.

The Iron Ghost's engines shifted tone. Acceleration. Kael watched the heading indicator swing starboard, watched the distance ticker begin its slow count downward, and felt something crack open in the silence he'd spent seven years constructing. Not loudly. Not with drama. Just the small, irreversible sound of a door he'd locked from the inside finally opening because the hand on the other side had learned how to call his name.

The scanner pulsed. Three times. The rhythm was clearer now, sharper, almost audible through the vacuum.

Almost like a voice.

Kael's fingers hovered over the navigation controls. He could still change course. He could kill the engines, turn the Iron Ghost back toward the thermal anomaly and the meaningless salvage that had kept him numb. He could choose the familiar emptiness over whatever was reaching toward him from the dark.

Instead, he locked in the coordinates and watched the distance counter spin downward. Thirty-one light-seconds. Thirty.

The void had waited seven years for him to stop running.

Now it was calling him back.

The distance collapsed. Twenty light-seconds. Fifteen. The scanner's resolution improved with each kilometer, and the signal began to resolve into something that made Kael's breath catch in a way he hadn't allowed himself to breathe in seven years.

A hull.

Not the jagged wreckage of a dead freighter or the uniform geometry of corporate architecture. This was something else—a sleek, elongated form that seemed to absorb the starlight rather than reflect it, matte-black and flawless, covered in what looked like crystalline growths or perhaps integral structures, impossible to tell which. The surface was smooth in a way that suggested it had never been designed for the vacuum to touch it, and yet here it was, intact, whole, impossibly preserved.

Eight hundred meters, his implant calculated. Maybe longer.

The bioluminescent runes began to resolve as he drew closer. Not painted on. Part of the hull itself. Faint blue-green pulses that seemed to follow no pattern he could identify, though his mind kept trying to find rhythm in them. A slow heartbeat, perhaps. Or a countdown. Or the biological signature of something that had been waiting so long for visitors that it had learned patience from the void itself.

Kael cut the Iron Ghost's acceleration. The ship groaned—a sound of metal and stress compensators adjusting to the sudden shift in momentum. He let the salvage operator in him take over, the part that knew how to approach unknown objects without triggering whatever defensive systems might still be active after millennia. Slow. Careful. Ready to burn engines and run if the first touch brought plasma and death.

The implant kept translating the signal. Still three pulses. Still the pause. Still the sense of something ancient reaching toward him with recognition, as if whatever had left this thing behind had built it specifically for a moment like this.

He should run. The rational part of him, the part that had kept him alive, was screaming it. Unknown alien technology. No way to know what it would do. No way to know if the signal was even real or just his implant misfiring, finally cracking under seven years of exile and silence.

Kael ran a diagnostic anyway. Nominal. All systems nominal. The signal was real.

He was still twelve light-seconds away when he made the decision. The suit hung in the locker where he'd left it months ago, the fabric stiff with disuse, the seals dusty. He ran through the precheck with mechanical precision—helmet, seals, oxygen, magnetic tethers—and cycled through the airlock without letting himself think too hard about what came next.

The void took him.

The Iron Ghost receded at his back, a small metal spark of warmth in the absolute cold. His suit's thermal indicators tried to compensate, pumping heated fluid through the layers of insulation, but space doesn't warm. Space doesn't negotiate. Space just takes and takes and takes until there's nothing left but the ghost of a person floating in the dark.

The alien hull grew larger.

It was warm.

Kael's gloved hand touched it first, a simple contact, the kind of thing he'd done a thousand times with derelict spacecraft and salvage points and the anonymous wreckage of human failure. But this was different. Through the suit material, through the insulation layers, through the thick rubber of the glove, he felt warmth. Actual heat. Radiating up from the crystalline surface like the skin of something still alive.

The bioluminescent runes brightened where his hand made contact.

His neural implant sang.

Not in the way of the signal—not three pulses, not a rhythm. A chord. A harmonic. A sound that existed only in the electrical impulses firing through his brain, translated by his implant into something almost musical. Something almost like recognition. Like the moment when a door opens and something on the other side says: finally. You're here. You're the one we've been waiting for.

Kael's breath came short in his helmet.

The runes spread across the hull in waves, following the path of his hand like neural pathways firing in sequence. More light. Brighter. Enough to cast sharp shadows across the crystalline surface, enough to show him that what he was looking at wasn't just wreckage. It was a message. It was a warning. It was a thing that had slept for longer than human civilization had been awake, and it had woken the moment his implant had come in range.

He pulled his hand back.

The runes faded slightly but didn't go dark. They kept pulsing, softer now, almost like breathing. The harmonic in his implant faded to a whisper, but it didn't stop. It was waiting. Patient. The way the void was patient.

Kael's magnetic tether was still attached to the Iron Ghost. He could fire the retraction mechanism right now. The ship would reel him in. He could be back in the airlock in under ninety seconds, could seal the hatch, could burn engines and run back toward the thermal anomaly and the meaningless salvage and the seven years of solitude that had kept him breathing but not alive.

The door was still open.

He pushed off the hull and drifted back toward the Iron Ghost, the alien ship receding behind him. The runes pulsed brighter as the distance increased. The harmonic in his implant grew louder, almost urgent, almost like it was calling after him. Come back. Come back. Don't go.

Kael didn't look back. He cycled through the airlock, peeled off the suit with shaking hands, and collapsed into the salvage operator's chair. His neural implant was still singing. Still waiting. Still reaching toward those coordinates with a hunger he hadn't felt in seven years because he'd spent seven years training himself not to feel anything at all.

The Iron Ghost was still pointing at those coordinates. The engines were still ready to accelerate. The decision had already been made the moment he'd left the pilot's seat to suit up.

There was no running from this.

He locked the navigation system, engaged the autopilot, and set the course for the alien hull. The ship lurched forward, and Kael didn't try to stop it. In the back of his mind, somewhere beneath the rational calculations and the fear and the strange, overwhelming sense of recognition that was tearing at the walls he'd built, he heard his own voice from seven years ago.

Never again. Never let anyone close. Never lead. Never trust.

The void had other plans.

The Iron Ghost accelerated toward the dark, and Kael Voss, for the first time since the screaming had stopped in the ice beneath Europa, chose to move toward something instead of away from it. The point of no return had passed an hour ago, maybe longer. Now there was only the forward motion, the strange harmonic in his implant, and the ancient ship that had been waiting in the dark for someone exactly like him to come close enough to touch.

The airlock opened to absolute silence.

Kael stepped through, magnetic boots engaging against the metal decking, and waited for the inner seal to hiss shut behind him. The alien hull had no internal atmosphere—his suit's readings confirmed what his instincts already knew. The cold was deeper here, pressed against him through the insulation like something with weight and intention. His breath fogged the helmet visor in quick, shallow clouds.

The chamber beyond the airlock was not a chamber. It was absence given form.

No walls. No visible floor. No ceiling that his suit lights could find. Just a vast, impossible darkness that extended in all directions, punctuated by crystalline structures that hung in the zero-g like frozen thoughts. They ranged from needle-thin lattices to geometric formations the size of buildings, and they all pulsed with that same faint bioluminescence he'd seen on the hull—blue-green, hypnotic, following patterns his mind kept trying to decode and failing.

His neural implant was screaming.

Not in pain. Not in the harmonic that had touched him on the hull. This was different. This was signal resolution pushed past its limits, data streams flooding faster than translation matrices could parse. Kael's vision flickered—actual sight overlaid with digital overlays, coordinates scrolling, mathematical notations that made no sense and somehow made perfect sense, a language his implant was learning in real-time.

He moved deeper into the chamber. His magnetic boots made no sound against the invisible deck—there was no deck, his senses told him, even as his feet found purchase on something solid. The contradiction didn't register as wrong anymore. Nothing about this was wrong. It was ancient. It was waiting. It was the reason his implant had been designed seven years ago with specs he'd never understood, upgrades that had never been fully explained in the discharge papers he'd never read carefully enough.

The device was at the chamber's center.

It hung in the absolute middle of the impossible space, and Kael knew—the way you know your own heartbeat without counting it—that the chamber had been built around it. Designed for it. Waiting for it to be found. The crystal was perfect geometry that shifted when he wasn't looking directly at it, a shape that existed in more dimensions than his eyes could process. It pulsed with a rhythm that matched the signature in his implant, matched his own heartbeat, matched something deeper than biology—something that felt like the pulse of time itself.

Kael's suit was already reading elevated cortisol. Adrenaline. Thermal stress. The rational part of him, the salvage operator, the survivor, was screaming warnings. This was exposure. This was the moment before something catastrophic. This was the threshold past which there was no return.

He moved toward the crystal anyway.

The distance was difficult to judge in the zero-g. A hundred meters might have been ten. The chamber might have been expanding around him as he approached, or he might have been shrinking. His suit's instruments kept adjusting their readings, unable to establish a stable baseline in the presence of the device. Only the rhythm was constant—the pulse that matched his heartbeat, growing louder as he drew closer, no longer a harmonic in his implant but something he could almost feel in his chest.

His gloved hand reached out.

The crystal was still three meters away. Then two. Then his hand was crossing the final distance and there was no way to stop it, no override in his nervous system that could prevent what was about to happen. Every instinct told him this was the moment his life ended. Every instinct also told him this was the moment his life actually began.

His fingers touched the surface.

The crystal ignited.

Not fire. Not heat. Light. Blue-white and overwhelming, so bright it burned through the suit's visor darkening and burned through his eyelids and burned through the back of his skull and filled the chamber with the kind of illumination that didn't come from photons but from the structure of reality itself being briefly, terribly exposed. Kael's scream was swallowed in his helmet. His neural implant exploded into something beyond sensation—not pain, not pleasure, but the overwhelming sensation of doors opening all at once in a structure he'd never known existed inside his own mind.

Data.

Not human data. Not corporate information streams or military databases or anything that could be filed or organized or made sense of in sequence. This was the unfiltered knowledge of something that had watched stars form and die. Coordinates burned across his vision—not just numbers but the *meaning* of them, the weight of space and time compressed into pure information. A location. Another location. Seventeen locations. Forty. Hundreds. All pulsing with the same rhythm, all calling with the same voice.

And underneath it all, a countdown.

Not visual. Not a number. A sensation in his chest like a second heartbeat, like something in the core of his being was ticking downward toward a moment he couldn't name. The device was still burning against his fingertips—he could feel it through the suit material, through the insulation, through layers that should have been impenetrable. It was warm. It was alive. It was pulling him deeper into its light.

Kael tried to pull his hand away.

The crystal held.

Not physically. His fingers were still his own, his arm still obeyed the basic impulses of his nervous system. But at some level beneath consciousness, beneath intention, the device was bonding with him. He could feel it interfacing with his neural implant—not as an external connection but as an integration, a merging, the way two frequencies align and become a single, stronger harmonic.

The countdown in his chest beat faster.

Warnings flooded his suit's diagnostic systems. Neural integrity compromised. Implant signature mutation detected. Biological-technological integration threshold exceeded. His suit was screaming the data equivalent of a death knell, but beneath it all, Kael was still alive. Still breathing. Still feeling the cold of the chamber and the warmth of the device and the overwhelming sense that he was the only person in the solar system who could have survived this moment.

Or the first.

Or the instrument that was being played by something that had learned patience from forty thousand years of waiting in the dark.

The light faded. Not gradually. All at once, as if a door had closed. Kael's eyes adjusted, and he was standing in the chamber again, his hand still touching the crystal, his neural implant still singing but in a language he could almost understand now. His fingers felt numb. His mind felt split, running parallel processes like his skull had become a ship with two captains.

The device released him.

Or he released it—the distinction had become meaningless. Kael pulled his hand back, and the crystal returned to its slow, patient pulsing. The chamber was no longer infinite. Now he could sense the walls, faint and crystalline, surrounding him on all sides. The device was no longer alone. It was the center of something vast and ancient and deeply, profoundly awake.

Kael's breathing came in controlled pulls, his suit's life-support systems compensating for the rapid depletion of oxygen. His neural implant was still processing the data, still learning the language the device had burned into his consciousness. But underneath it all, beneath the sensation of being split into two minds, he felt something else.

Recognition.

The device wasn't a weapon. The device was a lock, and Kael Voss had just become the key.

The countdown in his chest beat on, relentless and accelerating, and somewhere in the darkness of the solar system, something that had been sleeping in cold storage for longer than humanity had known how to build ships was finally, finally beginning to wake.

The countdown in his chest became a roar.

Not sound. Nothing so simple as acoustic vibration. This was information made physical, burning through his neural pathways like fire through old wood, and Kael's scream filled the chamber again—a sound that belonged to him and also didn't, as if his throat was translating something vast into the small, breakable shapes of human noise.

The visions came.

Not in sequence. Not in any order his mind could impose afterward. They simply *were*—flooding through the breach the device had torn in his consciousness, each image arriving with the weight of absolute certainty, the kind of knowing that didn't require understanding because it existed beneath understanding.

Coordinates.

Seventeen of them first. Then forty. Then more than he could count, spreading across the solar system like a constellation of warnings. Europa. Mars. The Belt. The outer stations. Each one pulsing with the same rhythm, the same terrible recognition. Each one *marked*.

And underneath the coordinates, a presence.

Not hostile. Not benign. Ancient. Something so old that the concept of time had become almost metaphorical to it, the way a human might think of geological epochs without feeling the weight of them. It had been sleeping. Now it was waking. And the waking was not gentle.

Kael saw the first colony die.

Not Europa—somewhere else, somewhere his implant had no reference for, but the knowledge was there anyway, burned into him by the device. A station. Three thousand people. The signal arriving like a wave, touching every neural implant simultaneously, and then the silence. Not death exactly. Cessation. The lights going dark all at once, the minds inside them simply *stopping*, the way a machine stops when you kill the power. Clean. Efficient. Final.

Then it was happening again. Different coordinates. Different colony. The same terrible wave of erasure spreading outward, and Kael understood with a clarity that was almost geological that he was watching the replay of something that had already happened. Not prediction. Memory. The device was showing him the past the way it had lived it—from a distance so vast that centuries became moments, and the death of thousands became a single data point in a pattern that had been unfolding for longer than human language had words for.

The warning came next.

Not words. Images that *meant* things. A shape in the darkness, vast and patient and moving with the inevitability of orbital mechanics. Something that had learned to travel between stars the way humans had learned to walk, and it was coming. It had always been coming. The device was the notification, the failsafe left behind by something that had understood, in the end, that it could not win. That all it could do was leave a warning and hope that whoever found it would be able to do what the ancient builders could not.

The coordinates burned brighter.

Kael understood suddenly, with a clarity that made him want to vomit, that each mark was a node. A network. And the device in his hand—the device he had touched, the device that was still singing through his neural implant like a second heartbeat—was the key that activated them all. The failsafe wasn't a weapon. It was a bell. And by touching it, by bonding with it, he had just rung it across the entire solar system.

The countdown accelerated.

Not in seconds. In some other metric, some unit of time that the ancient builders had used and that his implant was now translating into the only language it had: the rhythm of his own heartbeat, stretched and distorted and running faster, faster, faster. How long? his consciousness screamed. How long do we have?

The answer came not in time but in distance. The shape in the darkness was still far away—light-years, maybe, or the device was lying, or time didn't mean anything anymore because the shape was already *here* in some dimension his senses couldn't parse. It was moving. It was always moving. And it had been waiting for exactly this signal, this activation, this moment when something in the solar system finally woke up enough to acknowledge its presence.

Kael's vision fractured.

He was in the chamber and he was also in the Iron Ghost and he was also standing on a station he'd never seen, watching people's eyes go blank as the signal touched them. The device wasn't showing him the future. It was showing him the *pattern*. The rhythm of extinction applied to specific coordinates, specific populations, specific moments in time that were already carved into the structure of what was going to happen.

And he was the trigger.

That understanding hit him like physical impact. The device had chosen him. Not randomly. The implications burned through his implant like a second wave of data: his neural implant was compatible because it had been designed to be compatible. Someone in the corporate hierarchy, someone in a position of power seven years ago, had *known* this was coming. Had built him specifically to be a receiver, a carrier, a walking beacon for something ancient and patient and infinitely worse than any corporate conspiracy.

The visions began to fade.

Not gently. They were being pulled away, back through the device, back into the depths of whatever archive they'd come from. But fragments remained, stuck in his implant like shrapnel. Coordinates he could never forget. Warnings he couldn't unknow. And underneath it all, the terrible knowledge that his isolation—seven years of running, seven years of refusing to lead or trust or even acknowledge that other people existed—had been exactly what something had been waiting for.

A man alone was easier to use.

A man alone couldn't warn anyone.

A man alone was the perfect vessel for a message that would shatter anyone it touched.

His knees gave out. Kael fell through the zero-g of the chamber, his magnetic boots losing grip on the invisible deck, and he hung suspended in the darkness with the device still pulsing above him, still singing in his skull, still burning with the knowledge of what he'd just done.

The countdown continued.

Not in his chest anymore. Everywhere. In the structure of the chamber itself, in the crystalline structures around him, in the vast dark beyond the hull of the ancient ship. The device wasn't just a warning. It was a trigger. And by touching it, by letting it bond with his neural implant, Kael Voss had just started the clock on something that would either save humanity or erase it, and he had no way of knowing which one was actually true.

Only that it was coming.

Only that it was already moving.

Only that he had just become the only person in the solar system who knew why.

The distress signal arrived while Kael was still on his knees in the chamber, still processing the data burning through his implant like fire consuming a building from the inside out.

His suit's external comms crackled to life. Not human voices yet—just the carrier wave, the electronic ghost of transmission reaching across the dark. He pushed himself upright, magnetic boots engaging against the invisible deck, and pulled the signal stream into focus. The implant translated it faster than his conscious mind could follow: Europa Station. Research facility. Primary distress protocol.

Then the voice came through.

It was a woman. Young. Her words were coming in fragments, separated by static that sounded like screaming filtered through a thousand kilometers of vacuum. "—emergency shutdown, all systems—" "—can't reach anyone on Level Seven—" "—implants are—"

The transmission cut.

Kael waited. In the silence of the chamber, with the device still pulsing above him and the coordinates still burning across his vision, he waited for the next transmission. The next update. The reassurance that someone had managed to regain control, that this was a contained situation, that the colony was still intact and the people on it were still alive.

The silence stretched.

His neural implant fed him the data his conscious mind didn't want to accept. The distress beacon had been broadcasting for ninety seconds. No new transmissions in the last thirty. The colony's communication array was still operational—his implant could read the systems status from here, could see the data architecture still standing, the networks still humming with power. But no one was using them. No one was there to use them.

The news feeds began updating before the colony went completely dark.

He accessed them through the ship's systems, pulling feeds from the inner-system networks that still recognized his credentials as valid. The headlines were careful, corporate-polished, designed to contain panic: EUROPA STATION EXPERIENCES CATASTROPHIC SYSTEMS FAILURE. INVESTIGATION ONGOING. MINIMAL CASUALTIES REPORTED.

Minimal.

Kael's implant knew the truth. He could see it in the coordinates the device had shown him, could feel it in the countdown still accelerating in his chest like a second heartbeat. Europa was marked. Europe was *triggered*. And the signal wasn't something that spread through traditional networks or communications systems. It spread through neural implants. Every consciousness in that facility that had been enhanced with the mandatory corporate neural architecture had just been simultaneously, completely, utterly erased.

Three thousand people.

The exact number appeared in his implant with the weight of absolute certainty, pulled from the device's ancient knowledge or from the corporate records it had somehow accessed or from some source beyond both. Three thousand minds. Three thousand sets of eyes going blank. Three thousand people who had never done anything wrong except exist in the wrong place at the wrong time, their only crime being that they'd been marked on a map drawn forty thousand years ago by something that saw them as nothing more than data points in a pattern of extinction.

And he had woken the pattern.

The knowledge hit him like decompression, sudden and absolute. The visions the device had shown him—the replay of colonies dying, the signal spreading, the shape moving through the darkness—none of that had been prediction. It had been the moment he was living right now, shown to him from a perspective so distant and cold that billions of deaths became indistinguishable from the migration of dust. The device hadn't been a warning about what *might* happen. It had been the announcement that what was already happening had just begun.

He thought of the woman's voice cutting through the static. Of the people still in the colony the moment the signal touched them. Of the specific, terrible instant when their neural implants—the same technology that let them think, work, communicate, survive—became the instruments of their own erasure.

Kael's breathing came hard and fast, his suit's systems registering elevated cortisol, adrenaline, all the physiological markers of a man watching his worst fear become undeniable fact. Seven years. Seven years of isolation, of refusing to lead, of telling himself that disconnection was survival. Seven years of running from the ghost team, from the weight of command, from the terrible responsibility of having other people's lives depend on his choices. He had done it to protect them. He had done it to protect himself. And it had bought nothing. It had bought *time*, and the time had run out, and the moment it did, three thousand people he had never met burned away like paper in a fire he had lit.

His hands were shaking.

The distress beacon continued broadcasting, but there was nothing behind it now. Just the automated emergency protocol, the dying gasp of a system designed to call for help when the people who could hear that call were already gone. The Corporate Defense Alliance would respond. They would send a recovery ship. They would find the colony intact, the systems still operational, and absolutely nothing inside it but the bodies of people who had been dead for the last five minutes, their consciousness so thoroughly erased that they would never even understand what had happened to them.

And they would blame him.

The logical chain of causation was simple enough that even a corporate prosecutor could follow it. Kael Voss, wanted terrorist, had accessed a derelict alien structure. Kael Voss, with his illegal neural implant modifications, had activated something on that structure. Kael Voss, with his history of destabilization and violence, had somehow triggered the destruction of an entire research colony.

They would have evidence. They would have the data logs showing his implant's connection spike across the system. They would have the timing—the moment he touched the device to the moment the signal reached Europa, perfectly correlated, perfectly damning. They would have motive, opportunity, and the kind of narrative that corporate leadership could sell to the outer-rim populations: the dangerous rogue operative who finally showed his true nature.

What they would never understand was that he hadn't chosen this. That he had been chosen. That somewhere in the design specifications of his neural implant, seven years ago, someone in the corporate hierarchy had decided that he was the right instrument for this particular purpose—the perfect conduit for a message that would destroy anyone who heard it.

His isolation hadn't kept anyone safe.

It had only kept him isolated long enough to be useless when it mattered. Seven years of refusing to trust, seven years of cutting himself off from every human connection, seven years of telling himself that solitude was the highest form of responsibility—and it had all led to this moment, where the only thing his isolation had accomplished was to ensure that when he finally received a call he couldn't ignore, there was no one around to stop him from answering it.

Kael pulled up the ship's navigation systems. His hands were still shaking, but the calculations came easy, muscle memory from seven years of salvage runs and course corrections in deep space. The Iron Ghost was two days from Europa Station at standard acceleration. Two days to decide what to do. Two days to figure out how to explain to the authorities that he hadn't done this. Two days before they found him and killed him, or worse—worse because it was possible—they might believe him and ask him to explain what he had actually done.

The device continued its patient pulsing in his skull.

The countdown continued to accelerate.

And somewhere in the darkness beyond the solar system, something vast and ancient acknowledged the signal and continued its inevitable approach, patient as geological time, hungry as the void itself.
